extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Legal doctrinal guidance on (1) jurisdiction over patent questions in federal and state courts and (2) the rights, breaches, and remedies relating to unpatented (secret) inventions, including effects of confidential and public disclosure and the U.S. two-year statutory grace period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral inquiry by State courts into patent validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity, title, and infringement may be collaterally questioned in a State court (e.g., in suits upon notes, contracts for purchase-money of a patent-right, suits on licenses or for royalties), even though a State court cannot entertain a direct suit to repeal a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by cases such as Continental Store Service Co. v. Clark, Brown v. Texas Cactus Hedge Co., Keith v. Hobbs and others. Collateral questioning is permitted in actions where the patent issue arises incidentally to the contract or tort (e.g., defence to an action on a note given for a patent-right). The State court's inquiry may extend to identity of purpose and result and the utility of the invention (see Hunt v. Hoover). But the State court may not proceed in a direct action to invalidate a patent; collateral inquiry affects only the matter before that court (examples and caveats discussed).

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts cannot entertain direct suit to repeal a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A State court cannot entertain jurisdiction of a direct suit to repeal (cancel) a patent; a direct suit to repeal a patent must be brought in the appropriate federal forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although individuals have an abstract interest in seeing a void patent destroyed, that interest is insufficient to sustain a direct action in a State court to repeal a patent (citing cases such as Blatch. 866). State courts may examine validity only collaterally in appropriate actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts' power to punish contempt interfering with federal receivers and exclusive rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A State court may punish for contempt in interfering with a receiver of a corporation appointed by the court even when the interference consists of acts relating to an article the corporation has exclusive right to make; the State court will consider questions of jurisdiction and may dismiss/remand improperly instituted cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: where a receiver is making under order an article in which the corporation had an exclusive right, State courts have punished contempt for interference. However, jurisdictional issues must be timely raised (see discussion of timing below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Original federal jurisdiction over patent-law cases vested in circuit courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire original jurisdiction of the Federal courts over cases arising under the Patent Laws is vested in the Circuit courts, the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia, and such District courts as are endowed with Circuit court powers; the Supreme Court of the United States obtains jurisdiction by appeal from the Circuit Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts with circuit powers and the D.C. Supreme Court have the same powers in patent cases as Circuit courts. The Revised Statutes did not change the jurisdiction of the Circuit courts in patent cases (see Cochrane v. Deener).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of jurisdictional objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to jurisdiction must be taken before the pleadings are closed and the evidence published or they will be waived; subject-matter jurisdiction, however, is incurable and may be raised at any time and will result in dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an objection to jurisdiction is not timely asserted before pleadings are closed/evidence published, it may be waived to the extent parties can waive. But lack of subject-matter jurisdiction cannot be cured by laches and will be dismissed whenever discovered (cases: Teas v. Albright; Nesmith v. Calvert; Blanchard v. Sprague).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal courts will consider their jurisdiction and remand/dismiss improperly instituted cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts will always consider the question of their jurisdiction; a case erroneously brought from a State court will be remanded on motion, and a case improperly instituted in federal court will be dismissed or remanded to the appropriate tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Spring v. Domestic Sewing Mach. Co.; when federal courts find lack of jurisdiction they will dismiss (Blanchard v. Sprague) or remand (erroneously removed from State court).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's right to preserve secret rests on natural law
rubrics_metrics.description: The conception of an idea or means makes that idea the absolute and exclusive property of its conceiver until in some manner he communicates it to others; rights in an unpatented invention vest in the inventor by virtue of his inventive act alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Security of the inventor's property depends on his preservation of the secret; while he conceals the principle, it is incapable of imitation and his exclusive enjoyment is as perfect as if protected by positive law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forcible or fraudulent discovery of a secret invention violates inventor's rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The only wrong an inventor can sustain in respect to an entirely undisclosed invention is that by which his secret is wrested from him against his will — by force or fraud (including physical compulsion, threats, forcible invasion, asportation of the device, deceit or imposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms of wrong include violence/threats causing disclosure, physical invasion/seizure of device, or deceit inducing disclosure. The treatise treats these acts as torts actionable in the local courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for forcible or fraudulent discovery: damages and injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies must be sought in local courts via ordinary civil or equity procedure; compensation in damages is measured by ordinary rules, and equity may enjoin the defendant against use and communication of the invention's principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the secret cannot be restored, injunctions and damages can avert disastrous consequences and secure the inventor's practical enjoyment of the property. Remedies available both at law and in equity (authorities cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to preservation of secret when disclosed confidentially
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential communication of a secret invention (to employees, co-partners, others) does not destroy the inventor's right; those to whom it is communicated hold the knowledge in trust and are responsible to the inventor for compliance with imposed restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor may impart knowledge under pledges of secrecy or use restrictions; an invention thus communicated remains a secret invention regardless of how many have knowledge, provided disclosure was restricted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure or misuse by entrusted persons is breach of trust and actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: When those entrusted with a secret invention disclose or misuse it beyond authorized purposes, such acts constitute a breach of trust and are actionable (either as tort or contract).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrongful acquisition by outsiders (force/fraud) is a tort; misuse by those entrusted is breach of trust, actionable at law for damages and in equity for injunction. Examples and authorities cited (Peabody v. Norfolk, Salomon v. Hertz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for disclosure/misuse by entrusted persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The remedy is an action at law for damages in State or Federal courts (when jurisdiction exists) and equitable relief by injunction to prevent future unauthorized use or disclosure; executors and personal representatives may seek injunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions have been regarded either as torts (fraud) or contracts (express/implied). Equity will interpose when damages are inadequate and wrongful use would be irreparable (cases cited: Morison v. Moat, Green v. Folgham, Hammer v. Barnes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights exist even if the invention is not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor's rights in a secret invention and remedies for wrongs injuring that property are not dependent on Patent Law provisions; they exist equally whether the invention is or is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many inventive products lie outside statutory patentable classes yet are valuable; the creator may preserve secrecy and communicate confidentially and have the same redress for invasion as if the subject-matter were patentable (Peabody v. Norfolk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unrestricted disclosure forfeits the inventor's secret unless statute protects it
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of statute, unrestricted disclosure of a secret destroys the inventor's property in it — the idea passes into public possession and is dedicated to the public; method of disclosure (verbal, drawings, models, sale) is immaterial if disclosure is complete and voluntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unrestricted communication to one person gives that person the right to disseminate the information without limit and thereby permanently deprives the inventor of dominion over the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory two-year protection for public use and disclosure prior to application
rubrics_metrics.description: Under U.S. law an inventor may openly use and freely communicate a patentable invention for two years before his application (and during pendency of application) without forfeiting his right to patent protection; the inventor's situation after patent issuance is equivalent to having preserved secrecy until issuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory exception prevents the public from treating a permitted period of disclosure as abandonment, but questions remain about the nature of the inventor's property and available remedies during that disclosure period (the treatise discusses effects and competing views).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three competing views of inventor's rights during the statutory disclosure period
rubrics_metrics.description: Three possible views: (1) disclosure temporarily deprives inventor of vindicable property until patent issues (temporary abandonment/resumption); (2) disclosure does not affect property but suspends remedies until patent grant, with infringements actionable only after grant; (3) disclosure leaves invention with all attributes of a secret invention and inventor entitled to immediate remedies unless disclosure is protracted or accompanied by intent to abandon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise analyzes and rejects view (1) as untenable and finds significant objections to view (2). It outlines policy reasons, evidentiary presumptions about intent to abandon, and practical difficulties that counsel in favor of view (3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred doctrine: disclosure during the statutory period does not extinguish rights or remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The third view is the probable and preferred position: the inventor's property and immediate remedy rights are not affected by his unrestricted disclosure during the statutory period unless the disclosure is prolonged beyond the lawful period or accompanied by other acts showing intent to abandon; the invention retains the attributes of a secret invention during that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: consistent with the purpose of the statutory provision (to permit testing/public use without causing forfeiture), aligns with other inventor rights, avoids treating temporary authorized public use as irrevocable abandonment, and supports immediate remedies (law and equity) for invasion during the period. The statute was intended to extend inventor protections, not to create temporary public rights.
